Title: RM12,000 RMAF innovation delivers nearly RM150m in potential savings
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) has averted at least six potentially costly bird strike incidents involving its prized Su-30MKM fighter jets, saving nearly RM150 million in potential engine repair costs.
RMAF chief General Tan Sri Muhamad Norazlan Aris said the savings were made possible through a home-grown innovation developed jointly by the Aerospace Engineering Services Centre (Puspeka), No. 12 Squadron, Malaysian firms and universities, which reduced the risk of birds and other foreign objects being sucked into the Saturn AL-31FP engines during take-off and landing.
"The modest air intake screen (AIS) modification, which costs RM12,000, was designed to address one of the greatest hazards faced by fighter aircraft during take-off and landing — sucking in foreign objects, such as stones, debris or birds.
"Based on this innovation, we have saved millions of ringgit on engine repairs because whenever an engine is damaged, we have to send it back to its manufacturer and that costs a lot," he said in an exclusive interview with the
New Straits Times
.
In August last year, a RMAF F/A-18D Hornet fighter jet crashed in Kuantan shortly after takeoff from ingesting a bird into its left engine.
Norazlan said a fighter aircraft's engines generate tremendous suction during take-off as they draw in large volumes of air for combustion.
"When the engines spool up, they extract as much air as possible. Along with the air, they can also suck these foreign objects.
"In most cases, birds pose the biggest challenge. Because of their size, beaks and claws, if they are ingested into an engine operating at high speed, the damage can be severe."
Norazlan said the Su-30MKM was equipped with the AIS, which shielded the engines from foreign object damage while the aircraft was on the ground.
However, under the aircraft's original design, the protective screen automatically opens once the weight of the aircraft is off the wheels.
"At that point, the engines begin drawing in significantly more air, increasing the risk of bird ingestion.
"To overcome this vulnerability, RMAF engineers modified the system by installing additional relays that delay the opening of the AIS until after the aircraft has taken off and climbed to between 1,000 and 1,500 feet above ground level."
The modification also causes the screen to close earlier during landing.
Once the pilot lowers the landing gear on approach, the AIS closes automatically, protecting the engines throughout the remainder of the landing phase.
Norazlan said the effectiveness of the innovation had already been proven in service.
"There were occasions where, after landing, we found birds caught on the screen because it had remained closed. Had the screen opened earlier, those birds could have been ingested into the engines."
Norazlan said the innovation has not only reduced the risk of foreign object damage but also improved the operational availability of its frontline Su-30MKM fleet.

Title: Iran FM to visit Qatar for talks before UN assembly
Article:
TEHERAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was due for talks in Qatar, a key mediator in the US-Iran war, before travelling to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly, state media reported Sunday.
The minister "left Teheran on Sunday evening bound for New York... and will make a brief stop in Doha to hold consultations on the latest developments in the region," state news agency IRNA reported.
The stop in Doha comes as Iranian officials say they have once again stated through mediators Teheran's conditions for ending its blockade of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
The issue of the Hormuz strait has been central to the ongoing Middle East war that began in late February. Teheran blockaded it in response to the US-Israeli attacks.
Teheran now requires vessels to obtain its authorisation to pass through the strait, citing security and sovereignty concerns, and is considering a mechanism to impose service fees.
In response, the US has imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports as the conflict remains deadlocked.

Title: Evolving threats push RMAF to strengthen maritime watch
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Developments across strategic waterways globally are prompting  Malaysia to keep a watchful eye on its vast maritime areas, where threats to critical routes such as the South China Sea and Strait of Malacca could affect both national security and economic interests.
Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) chief General Tan Sri Muhamad Norazlan Aris told the
New Straits Times
that the service must place greater emphasis on maintaining an aerial watch over the country's waters as maritime security challenges continued to evolve.
"Malaysia's maritime security challenges today are increasingly complex and multifaceted. As a maritime nation, it depends heavily on sea lines of communication for trade, resource security and economic stability," he said.
"Therefore, any disruption in strategic areas such as the South China Sea and the Strait of Malacca would have a direct impact on national sovereignty and prosperity."
A CHANGING SECURITY LANDSCAPE
Norazlan said the main challenge begins with disputes and pressure from major powers in the South China Sea, imposing continuous stress on Malaysia's maritime sovereignty.
"This area continues to witness the presence of foreign coast guard vessels and research ships within the country's Exclusive Economic Zone.
"Studies by the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute indicate that 'grey zone' activities, such as aggressive patrols without open conflict, have increased in recent decades.
"At the same time, non-traditional threats have shown a significant rise. Illegal fishing activities by foreign vessels, particularly in the waters of Sabah and Sarawak, continue to occur repeatedly as data from the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) also points to hundreds of arrests each year.
"These activities not only deplete national fishery resources but are also linked to transnational crimes such as smuggling and human trafficking, thereby increasing the complexity of maritime security management."
Norazlan said the same goes for the Strait of Malacca, where more than 80 per cent of Malaysia's trade passes through it.
"This high traffic density also increases security risks. Reports by the International Maritime Bureau show that petty theft and attempted piracy incidents still occur periodically.
"This situation requires continuous monitoring and effective response measures to ensure the safety of maritime navigation."
He added that the increasing use of drones and unmanned systems has further complicated maritime security operations by making potential threats more difficult to detect through conventional surveillance methods.
RMAF EXPANDS ROLE IN SECURING MALAYSIA'S WATERS
Norazlan said  RMAF now plays a far greater role than conventional air defence, standing at
the forefront of national maritime security through integrated surveillance and rapid response capabilities.
He said  RMAF has strengthened its role as a force multiplier for the Royal Malaysian Navy (RMN) and MMEA through the sharing of air information and integrated surveillance capabilities.
"RMAF's long-range radar network, Control and Reporting Centres, Regional Air Operations Centres  and command-and-control systems allow it to generate a near real-time air and surface 'picture' to support operational decisions.
"These capabilities have enabled the early detection of aircraft movements and maritime activities, supporting faster operational decision-making and responses."
Norazlan said future capability development would continue to address both conventional and non-traditional threats through an integrated approach encompassing doctrine, personnel, assets and technology.
He said effective maritime surveillance also depended on close cooperation between  RMAF, RMN, MMEA and other government agencies under a whole-of-government approach.
Continuous investment in technology and human capital is essential, particularly in areas such as cyber operations, data analysis and system integration.
"As geopolitical competition intensifies in the Indo-Pacific, maintaining comprehensive maritime awareness is becoming increasingly important for countries seeking to protect  their sovereignty and economic interests.
"For Malaysia, safeguarding its maritime domain now extends beyond defending territorial waters. It increasingly requires the ability to detect emerging threats early, integrate intelligence across multiple agencies and maintain a credible presence across some of the world's busiest and most strategically contested sea lanes."
Norazlan also said it maintained a quick reaction alert  readiness to allow fighter aircraft to be deployed within a short timeframe, while regular patrols over strategic areas, such as Beting Patinggi Ali, served as a deterrent through continued presence.
CAPABILITY GAPS DRIVE MODERNISATION
Norazlan described  RMAF's current maritime surveillance capability as credible, but said it remained in a phase of transformation towards becoming a fully integrated, technology-driven force under the Capability Development Plan 2055 (CAP55).
[[nid:1537263]]
"Several challenges remain, particularly surveillance gaps across the vast maritime areas of Sabah and Sarawak, as well as limitations in the endurance and sensor capabilities of existing assets.
"These factors have been incorporated into  RMAF's long-term capability planning under CAP55."
Norazlan said areas of priority include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities through the acquisition of maritime patrol aircraft, medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial systems and modern sensor technologies.
In June, RMAF officially inducted and deployed its new Turkish-made TAI Anka-S drone at Labuan Air Base to conduct maritime surveillance over the South China Sea.
Norazlan added that the air force was also prioritising expanded radar coverage in East Malaysia, stronger ISR integration, greater interoperability with other agencies and continued investment in highly skilled personnel capable of operating advanced systems.
"Collectively, these initiatives reflect the RMAF's shift towards a layered surveillance network capable of detecting, tracking and responding to threats across both the air and maritime domains."
FROM 'SEE AND REPORT' TO OPERATIONAL RESPONSE
In keeping Malaysia's maritime domain secured, Norazlan said a key element of that transformation is the acquisition of the Leonardo ATR-72 maritime patrol aircraft (MPA) which is set to be delivered next year.
He said the aircraft would also support anti-surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare and search-and-rescue operations, enabling faster detection, tracking and response to both conventional and non-traditional threats, including foreign military incursions, smuggling, human trafficking and illegal fishing.
Norazlan said the ATR72 represented a significant capability enhancement over the  CN235 maritime surveillance aircraft.
"While the CN235 primarily performs surveillance and monitoring functions, the ATR-72 MPA extends beyond simply building maritime situational awareness. Instead, it is a transition from 'see and report' to 'see, track and support action'."
Equipped with more advanced sensors and greater endurance, the aircraft will be capable of conducting continuous ISR operations across the country while improving early detection of suspicious maritime activities.
"The acquisition reflects Malaysia's growing emphasis on persistent surveillance, allowing security agencies to maintain a clearer picture of activities across the country's vast maritime domain rather than reacting only after incidents occur."
